note: Event cards typed by Orbis from the cited Wikipedia articles. Dates are Gregorian; cards marked Julian show the Julian date their sources use (England kept the Julian calendar until 1752).

items.title: Alfred becomes king of Wessex
items.text: Alfred became king of the West Saxons in 871, in the middle of the Viking wars. By the 880s he called himself king of the Anglo-Saxons; his grandson Æthelstan ruled all England from 927.

items.title: Æthelstan, first king of all England
items.text: At Eamont, near Penrith, the kings of Scotland, Strathclyde and Bamburgh accepted Æthelstan's rule on 12 July 927. Historians count him as the first king of England.

items.title: Cnut, a Danish king of England
items.text: After Edmund Ironside died in November 1016, the Danish prince Cnut became king of all England. He later ruled Denmark and Norway too.

items.title: Battle of Stamford Bridge
items.text: Harold II defeated the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada, who had invaded with Harold's brother Tostig. Three days later William of Normandy landed in the south.

items.title: Battle of Hastings
items.text: William, Duke of Normandy, defeated and killed Harold II. He was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066, and Norman lords replaced most of the English nobility.

items.title: Henry II: the first Plantagenet
items.text: Henry, Count of Anjou and Duke of Normandy, and through his wife Duke of Aquitaine, became king of England in 1154. He ruled more of France than the French king; he died at Chinon in 1189.

items.title: Normandy lost
items.text: King John lost Normandy to Philip II of France when Rouen surrendered in 1204. English kings kept Gascony, around Bordeaux, until 1453.

items.title: Magna Carta
items.text: Barons in revolt made King John agree a charter at Runnymede that limited royal power. The Pope annulled it within weeks, but it was reissued and became a founding text of English law.

items.title: Battle of Agincourt
items.text: Henry V of Lancaster defeated a larger French army. By the Treaty of Troyes in 1420 he was to inherit the French crown, but he died in 1422 and France was lost by 1453.

items.title: Wars of the Roses end at Bosworth
items.text: Henry Tudor, heir of the Lancastrian claim, defeated and killed Richard III of York. He married Elizabeth of York, uniting the two houses; the Tudor rose joins their emblems.

items.title: Henry VIII heads the Church
items.text: The Act of Supremacy made the king Supreme Head of the Church of England, ending the Pope's authority after Rome refused to annul Henry's first marriage.

items.title: Calais, the last foothold in France, is lost
items.text: France took Calais from Mary I. English kings had held it since 1347.

items.title: Union of the Crowns
items.text: Elizabeth I died childless. Her cousin James VI, king of Scotland since 1567, became James I of England: one king, but still two kingdoms with their own parliaments.

items.title: Charles I executed
items.text: After two civil wars, Parliament tried the king and beheaded him outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall. England was ruled without a king until 1660.

items.title: The Restoration
items.text: Charles II, son of the executed king, returned to London on his 30th birthday and took the throne.

items.title: The Glorious Revolution
items.text: The Dutch stadtholder William of Orange landed at Brixham with an army; the Catholic James II fled. In 1689 William III and Mary II were offered the crown together with the Bill of Rights.

items.title: Act of Settlement
items.text: Parliament settled the crown on Sophia of Hanover, a granddaughter of James I, and her Protestant heirs, passing over closer Catholic relatives. Every monarch since descends from her.

items.title: Acts of Union: Great Britain
items.text: England and Scotland merged into one Kingdom of Great Britain with one parliament at Westminster. Scotland kept its own law and church.

items.title: George I: a German king
items.text: Queen Anne died; Sophia had died weeks before, so her son George, Elector of Hanover, became king. Britain and Hanover shared a ruler until 1837.

items.title: Union with Ireland
items.text: The Kingdom of Ireland merged with Great Britain into the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland; the Irish parliament in Dublin closed.

items.title: Hanover goes its own way
items.text: Victoria became queen of the UK, but Hanover's law barred women while a male heir lived, so her uncle Ernest Augustus became king of Hanover.

items.title: Windsor
items.text: In the middle of the war with Germany, George V renamed the royal house from Saxe-Coburg and Gotha to Windsor, after the castle.

items.title: Edward VIII abdicates
items.text: Edward VIII gave up the throne to marry Wallis Simpson, an American divorcée; his brother became George VI.

items.title: Charles III
items.text: Elizabeth II died at Balmoral after 70 years on the throne, the longest reign in British history. Her son became Charles III.
items.source: Wikipedia, 'Death and state funeral of Elizabeth II'
